sites.name: Galena Creek rock glacier
sites.coordNote: Approximate; not yet taken from a primary source
sites.label: established
sites.labelNote: Papers in 2020 and 2026. The 2026 work calls these glaciers some of the best analogs.
sites.role: Lead Mars story: the only pair where the same quantity, ice purity, has been estimated on both worlds.
sites.claim: Both are bodies of nearly pure ice buried under a thin layer of rock debris.

figures.q: How pure the buried ice is
figures.earthNote: Estimated from how fast the glacier flows, not from cores
figures.otherNote: Regional radar survey of the debris aprons

figures.earthNote: Upper section. Drone radar matched digging and drilling
figures.otherNote: We found no checked figure for Mars

matches.t: Galena Creek carries rock debris 1 to 1.5 m thick on its upper section, over ice estimated at 80 to 95% pure.
Radar shows the debris aprons of Deuteronilus Mensae are more than 80% water ice.
Deuteronilus Mensae and Arcadia Planitia are named as where ice on Mars is most accessible.

breaks.t: The Earth figure is inferred from flow speed. Nobody has cored the ice to check it.
Debris thickness on Mars is not verified, and that thickness decides how reachable the water is.
Scale: one glacier 1.6 km long against debris aprons surveyed across a whole region.
Wyoming is far warmer, has liquid water in summer, and has life.
Terrain was not measured for this pair. The open Mars elevation grid is too coarse to resolve a 1.6 km glacier.

sites.helps: Drone radar at Galena Creek measured debris thickness that matched digging and drilling. On Mars, that thickness decides how reachable the water is for a crew.
sites.data: Published radar and glaciology; no terrain run

terrain: Not measured: the open Mars grid is too coarse for a 1.6 km glacier
temp: Warmer, with liquid water in summer
ice: Ice under 1 to 1.5 m of debris, estimated 80 to 95% pure
sub: Buried ice body sounded by radar
ops: Radar method for finding drillable ice

sites.name: Kamestastin Lake impact structure
sites.label: established
sites.labelNote: Used by space agencies: astronauts trained here in September 2021.
sites.role: The one pair with measured terrain on both worlds.
sites.claim: Alike in rock, unlike in terrain: the same anorthosite as the lunar highlands, in a crater far shallower and gentler than de Gerlache.
sites.terrainVerdict: Measured, and it does not match. On the same 80 m grid the lunar crater has many times the relief and much steeper slopes.
sites.terrainReading: Our reading, not tested here: Kamestastin has had about 36 million years of weather and holds a lake; de Gerlache has had no weather at all. The controls on the Method page show these measures capture ruggedness, not shape: they cannot tell a crater from a dune field.

matches.t: A 28 km impact crater about 36 million years old.
Formed in anorthosite, the main rock of the lunar highlands.
One of only two craters on Earth with substantial anorthosite.
Astronauts trained here in September 2021.

breaks.t: Terrain, measured: the two craters do not have similar relief or slopes. See the numbers above.
A lake-filled site with water, weather and life.
Soil, temperature and lighting do not match.
The elevation model cannot see under the lake or the forest. The lake is masked out of every measure.

sites.helps: Sampling of impact rocks, traverse planning and crew geology training.
sites.prior: Not new: this is an agency training site.

geo: Formed in anorthosite, the main rock of the lunar highlands
terrain: Measured on one 80 m grid, and it does not match: de Gerlache is far deeper and steeper
temp: Subarctic; nothing like polar cold traps or low sun
ice: A lake and seasonal snow, not cold-trapped ice
dust: Soil and glacial deposits, not regolith
ops: Share of ground under the 8° landing tilt limit, measured on both. Far more of Kamestastin is gentle

sites.cmpNote: Anchor and analog wording is taken from this site's notes; it is not independently sourced.
sites.tcoordNote: The Gazetteer lists three centres; this is the first, and the one the terrain window was cut at. Diameter 32.71 km

sites.name: Sittampundi anorthosite complex
sites.tcoordNote: Approximate pin on the ridge between Shackleton and de Gerlache, not from a primary source. The soil claim is regional
sites.label: established
sites.labelNote: Established as a source of simulant. Unstudied as a field site.
sites.claim: The rock matches the composition of lunar highland soil. Nothing else about the place does.

matches.t: ISRO's lunar soil simulant, made from this rock, has major oxides mostly equivalent to lunar highland anorthosite.
The simulant is reported as comparable with Apollo 16 samples.
Chandrayaan-3 found 23 south-polar soil samples to be mostly ferroan anorthosite.

breaks.t: Composition only. It says nothing about temperature, lighting or volatiles.
A tropical, vegetated, inhabited place.
No study of Sittampundi as a field analog site was found, only as a source of rock.

sites.helps: Bulk material for landing and rover tests. ISRO needed 60 to 70 tonnes.
sites.prior: One paper and a patent on the simulant.

geo: Simulant oxides close to highland anorthosite
dust: Crushed rock stands in for regolith in tests
ops: Bulk simulant for landing and wheel tests

sites.coordNote: Point seen in a search result only (Mindat). The 1963 paper places the complex within 77°45′ to 78°5′ E, near 11°10′ N

sites.name: Umm Jirsan lava tube
sites.label: hypothesis
sites.labelNote: Our proposal. No study of it as a lunar-pit analog was found, and no measurement tests it.
sites.claim: A large, dry lava tube that could stand in for a lunar pit. Nobody has measured whether it does.

figures.earth: 8 to 12 m high, up to 45 m wide
figures.earthNote: 1,481 m of passage in three segments
The site paper gives none, and none was found elsewhere
figures.otherNote: In the permanently shadowed part of the pit

matches.t: 1,481 m of passage, 8 to 12 m high and up to 45 m wide, in three segments split by two collapses.
A dry site: under 100 mm of rain a year.
Lunar pits are described as thermally stable places that could shelter crews.

breaks.t: Scale: the lunar pit is about 100 m deep; the tube is 8 to 12 m high.
No interior temperature or humidity has been published for Umm Jirsan, so the property that makes a lunar pit useful is untested here.
The site paper is archaeology. It has no Moon or Mars content.

sites.helps: Testing skylight entry, cave mapping and radio relay, and measuring how well the tube buffers temperature.
sites.prior: None found as a lunar-pit analog, including in three further searches on 15 November. A 2026 review frames Saudi volcanic fields as analogs for icy moons, so the claim of novelty is only this narrow.
sites.data: The 2024 survey paper; NASA on lunar pits

geo: Basalt tube; the lunar pit is in mare basalt
sub: Proposed by us as a lunar-pit analog. Tube 8 to 12 m high; the pit is about 100 m deep
ops: Proposed: cave access, mapping and radio relay tests

sites.tcoordNote: Depth 105 m in the LROC pits list

sites.name: Great Kobuk Sand Dunes
sites.coordNote: Approximate; not yet taken from a primary source
sites.label: established
sites.role: A process, with a satellite record behind it.
sites.claim: Cold-climate dunes that researchers chose as the closest match to the dune fields around Mars's north pole.

matches.t: Chosen by researchers as most similar to Mars's north polar dune fields.
The dunes moved 1.3 m a year from 2003 to 2008.
Snow covers them for about two-thirds of the year.

breaks.t: Liquid water persists under the dunes all year.
The site may be less useful as its permafrost warms.

sites.helps: Change detection from orbit, and mobility on frozen sand.
sites.data: Literature only; no Mars dataset chosen

temp: Snow-covered for most of the year
dust: Dunes moved about 1.3 m a year, 2003 to 2008
bio: Liquid water persists under the dunes
ops: Change detection and mobility on frozen sand

sites.tcoordNote: Centre of Olympia Undae, the north polar dune field

sites.name: Bodélé Depression
sites.target: Dust lifting on Mars (a process, no single place)
sites.label: hypothesis
sites.labelNote: Our proposal, and a narrow one: Bodélé for dust lifting. The area is already a published Mars analog for other processes.
sites.claim: The dustiest place on Earth, proposed here as a test bed for how dust is lifted on Mars.

matches.t: A former lake bed that produces about half the mineral dust leaving the Sahara.
Mountains funnel the wind across it.
The dust forms as flakes of diatomite wear each other down.

breaks.t: The dust is the remains of freshwater diatoms: it comes from life.
How dust lifting differs in Mars's thin air is not verified.
Novelty is narrow. Bodélé is already in the Mars literature for yardangs and dunes; only the dust-lifting pairing is ours.

sites.helps: Testing dust-emission models and storm forecasting.
sites.prior: We found no published study that uses the Bodélé Depression as an analog for dust lifting on Mars. It is not new as a Mars analog in general: the area around it has been used as an analogue for dunes carving yardangs in Becquerel crater, and dunes north-east of it were compared with dunes at Hellespontus Montes. The search could not read paywalled full texts.

geo: Its yardangs and dunes have been compared with Martian ones. The diatomite itself has no Mars counterpart
dust: Proposed by us for Mars dust lifting. On Earth it supplies about half the dust leaving the Sahara
bio: The dust itself is from water life
ops: Proposed: dust forecasting for surface operations

sites.name: Lake Salda
sites.label: benchmark
sites.role: The benchmark the other pairs are held against.
sites.claim: A well-studied pair: a living carbonate lake set against the ancient lake of Jezero.

matches.t: An alkaline lake about 196 m deep and 7 km across, in an ultramafic catchment, where hydrous magnesium carbonates are the main precipitates.
Jezero held a lake 45 km across and has hydrated magnesium carbonate deposits.

breaks.t: Modern and biologically active. It cannot show long exposure, burial or the slow changes rock goes through afterwards.

sites.helps: Biosignature search strategy, and recognising deposit types.
sites.prior: Well known. Shown as a benchmark, not as a find.

geo: Magnesium carbonates, as found at Jezero
bio: Living lake: tests biosignature strategy, not ancient Mars

sites.name: Matanomadh Formation
sites.label: established
sites.labelNote: Published as a Mars analog in 2014 and 2025. Label assigned by us from that record.
sites.role: On the map with its cited evidence. Not measured: no matching open mineral data was confirmed for both worlds.
sites.claim: Iron sulfates of the kind reported from Meridiani Planum, in sediments laid over basalt.

matches.t: Jarosite with gypsum, an association also reported from Meridiani Planum, and with goethite, in sediments over Deccan basalts.
A later paper finds natrojarosite with natroalunite and kaolinite.

breaks.t: It is the sodium form of jarosite.
The two sources disagree on how it formed.

sites.helps: Calibrating spectral and X-ray instruments on mixtures of sulfates and clays.

geo: Jarosite with gypsum, as reported from Meridiani

sites.coordNote: The village of Mata no Madh, not the outcrop. No primary source gave the outcrop's position
sites.tcoordNote: Opportunity rover landing site, Meridiani Planum

sites.name: Azerbaijan mud volcanoes
sites.target: Mound fields of Chryse and Acidalia
sites.label: established
sites.labelNote: Niche but established in the Mars literature.
sites.role: On the map with its cited evidence. Not measured.
sites.claim: Mud volcanoes compared in the literature with fields of cones and mounds on the northern plains of Mars.

matches.t: Cones in Chryse up to over 1 km wide were compared with Azerbaijani mud volcanoes.
The mapped parts of southern Acidalia have over 18,000 mounds; Azerbaijan has 20 to 40 eruptive centres per 1,000 square km.

breaks.t: The 2010 study used edifices under tens of metres wide.
The NASA abstract names submarine mud volcanoes in the Gulf of Cadiz as the closest match in shape.

sites.helps: Sampling fine sediment brought up from depth, and methane sensing.
sites.prior: Used as analogs for possible sedimentary volcanoes on Mars.

geo: Mud volcano landforms compared with Martian cones and mounds
sub: Mud brings fine sediment up from depth

sites.coordNote: Bozdag Gobu mud volcano, one of the province's volcanoes. The volcano named in the Mars comparison could not be located
sites.tcoordNote: Centre of Acidalia Planitia. The mounds were mapped across its southern part

sites.name: Makgadikgadi Pans
sites.target: Lake deposits of Gale and Jezero
sites.label: established
sites.labelNote: Discussed as an analogue for Martian playas in a 2023 paper and a 2026 abstract. Label assigned by us from that record.
sites.role: On the map with its cited evidence. Not measured.
sites.claim: One of Earth's largest salt-pan systems, set against the dried lake deposits of Gale and Jezero.

matches.t: One of Earth's largest evaporite systems, considered an analogue for Martian playas.
Satellite spectra show clays and evaporites. The result is described as preliminary.

breaks.t: The abstract compares it with orbital spectra of Jezero and Gale but reports no results.

sites.prior: A 2023 paper discusses the pans' implications for Martian playa environments, and a 2026 abstract compares them with Jezero and Gale. Other papers were seen in search results and not checked.

geo: Clays and evaporites from satellite spectra, preliminary

sites.coordNote: Centre of the pans as given in a 2023 paper
sites.tcoordNote: Pin placed at the centre of Gale crater

sites.name: Río Tinto mining district
sites.coordNote: Town of Minas de Riotinto; a tertiary source
sites.label: benchmark
sites.labelNote: A long-studied analog, shown for context.
sites.confidence: Not rated: outside the source check
sites.role: Added by the team after the source check. Its paper was confirmed on 15 November, by abstract only.
sites.claim: An acid river system whose iron sulfates and oxides are a partial analog of the rocks at Meridiani Planum.
sites.scale: A river basin, not yet sized

matches.t: Iron-rich jarosite and hematite deposits, a partial sedimentary analog of the Meridiani rocks.
Traces of microbial life are preserved as textures in the iron oxides.

sites.helps: Practice reading iron-sulfate rocks like those at Meridiani Planum, including how traces of life survive in them.

bio: Traces of microbial life preserved in iron oxides

sites.name: Yungay area, Atacama Desert
sites.coordNote: A regional point for the Atacama, not Yungay itself
sites.tcoordNote: Sources differ by up to about 0.4 degrees
sites.label: benchmark
sites.labelNote: A long-studied analog, shown for context.
sites.confidence: Not rated: outside the source check
sites.role: Added by the team after the source check. Its paper was confirmed on 15 November, by abstract only.
sites.claim: Soil so dry and so poor in organic matter that it was described as Mars-like.

matches.t: Very dry, salty soils with almost no organic matter, described as Mars-like.
Almost no culturable microbes; the soil breaks organics down without life.

sites.helps: Tests whether Viking-type instruments would find organics in very dry, oxidising soil.

ice: Driest core of the Atacama; dry enough to limit microbial life
bio: Almost no culturable microbes; soil breaks organics down without life

limitsHead: What no Earth site can reproduce
limits: The Moon pulls at 1.62 m/s² and Mars at 3.73 m/s². Earth pulls at 9.82 m/s² everywhere.
The Moon has essentially no atmosphere.
About 0.6 kPa at the surface of Mars, under 1% of Earth's 101.4 kPa.
Neither world has Earth's shielding. No Earth site reproduces either radiation environment.
limitsNote: Each site stands in only for the characteristics listed on its page.

negative.head: The negative result
negative.text: No natural Earth site was found that reproduces the cold, the lighting or the volatiles of the lunar south pole. A permanently shadowed part of Cabeus crater averages 37 K. The Moon candidates here match rock and caves only.

earth.name: Earth
earth.desc: Our test bench. Each site here matches the Moon or Mars in some measured or documented ways and differs in others.
earth.sitesHead: Earth sites and processes in this atlas
earth.limit: Liquid water, weather and life act on every Earth site and alter it in ways the Moon and Mars do not.

moon.name: Moon
moon.desc: Airless and grey, with highlands of pale anorthosite and craters that have barely eroded in billions of years. The south pole is where Artemis plans to land.
moon.limit: One sixth of Earth gravity, a vacuum, unshielded radiation, and the cold and lighting of polar craters. No Earth site matches these.

mars.name: Mars
mars.desc: A cold desert with a thin carbon dioxide atmosphere, buried ice, dune fields and old lake beds that record a wetter past.
mars.limit: About a third of Earth gravity, air under 1% as dense, high radiation and no liquid water at the surface today.

planetsNote: Figures: NASA Planetary Fact Sheets for Earth, the Moon and Mars, read on 15 November 2026.

operations: Gentle ground is the share of each window with a slope under 8°, the tilt NASA's Human Landing System must tolerate for surface operations. That requirement gives no baseline and site studies apply it at about 5 m, so on our 80 m grid this is a coarse screen, not a landing-safety assessment. Ground under 8° is also under the rover limits we found (VIPER 15°).
breaks: Shape only. Gravity, vacuum, temperature, lighting and erosion all differ, and the elevation model cannot see under the lake or the forest.
imagery: Imagery: NASA GIBS Blue Marble; LRO WAC global mosaic and Viking MDIM 2.1 colour mosaic through NASA Trek. NASA is acknowledged as the source and does not endorse this project.

p: Every page argues one thing: this place on Earth is like that place on the Moon or Mars in these ways, and unlike it in these.

Terrain is the only property we could measure the same way on both worlds with open data, so it is the only one we measure. Every other dimension is shown as cited evidence, with a link to its source.
There is no combined score. Each measure is shown on its own, with a plain ratio, so no single number hides its parts.

ul: Benchmark: a well-studied pair, shown for comparison. Not new.
Established: published as an analog, or used by a space agency. Not new.
Hypothesis: proposed by us. Not published as this analog and not tested. A hypothesis is never shown as a finding.
Measured: the same quantity, from data, on both worlds. Today that is terrain only.
Cited: a published source says so. The link is on the page.
Partial match: alike in kind only.
Hypothesis: our proposal, not published and not tested.
Breaks here: known not to match.
Not assessed: nobody on the team has checked. This is an allowed answer, and an empty cell is never filled by a guess.

p: Both windows are 40 km squares. Each is area-averaged onto one 80 m grid before anything is measured, because slope depends on the distance between samples: two terrains are only comparable at one resolution. Slope is computed from height differences in metres.
ul: Relief: 95th minus 5th percentile height of the unmasked cells.
Median slope and 95th percentile slope, in degrees.
Roughness: the spread of height left after removing a 5 by 5 cell (400 m) moving average.

Gentle ground: the share of unmasked cells with a slope under 8°. That is the tilt NASA's Human Landing System must tolerate for surface operations (Chavers et al. 2020; NASA Inspector General report IG-26-004). The requirement gives no baseline and site studies apply it at about 5 m, so at 80 m this is a coarse screen, not a landing-safety assessment.
Slope histogram: 2 degree bins from 0 to 40, the same bins on both sides.
p2: Earth: Copernicus DEM GLO-30, read from Microsoft Planetary Computer and reprojected to UTM zone 20N at 30 m, with the lake masked. Moon: LRO LOLA polar gridded elevation LDEM_80S_80M at 80 m, with every scale factor and offset read from the product label.

The measures are computed in Python and written to a file. The browser draws what is in the file and never invents or recomputes a measurement. The script checks itself on made-up terrain first: a flat plane must give zero slope, and a uniform 20 degree ramp must read as 20 degrees.

p: The elevation model stores the lake surface, not the lake bed, and the top of the forest, not the ground under it. The lake is masked out of every measure.
Shape says nothing about gravity, vacuum, temperature, lighting, or what the ground is made of.

The measures should agree on terrains that are alike and separate terrains that are not. We ran the same measures on five 40 km windows: two lunar craters, Kamestastin, a dune field and a flat lake bed.
ul: Two lunar craters measure alike, as expected.
A flat lake bed is clearly different from every crater, as expected.
A dune field is not separated from Kamestastin. On these measures the Earth crater sits closer to the dunes than to either lunar crater.
p2: What that means: relief, slope and roughness describe how rugged the ground is, not what shape it has. They show that Kamestastin is far gentler than de Gerlache. They cannot show whether ground is crater-shaped. A measure of shape, such as a crater's depth against its width, is the next thing to add.

The two control windows were placed by us, not taken from a source: Sua Pan near 20.75° S, 25.95° E, and the Namib Sand Sea near 24.75° S, 15.30° E. In the Sua Pan window the notebook's lake test masked 0.4% of the cells.

p: The research behind the candidate list made 416 factual claims. Each was checked against the source it cited: 391 were supported, 23 were not and were corrected or removed, and 2 sources could not be opened.

The limits of that check: much of the evidence is abstracts and press releases, and most pages were read through a tool that returns a summary of the page, not its raw text. The source list below says how much of each source was read.

Río Tinto and Yungay were added by the team after that check. Their two papers were confirmed on 15 November, by abstract only. Coordinates, the slope limit and the Bodélé literature search were also added on 15 November; their sources carry ids starting with R, G or F.
This site was built with an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic), directed by the team. The assistant did the literature research and the source check, drafted the text, and wrote most of the code.

An AI assistant can state a wrong fact with confidence. That is why every claim here carries a link to its source, the source list says how much of each source was actually read, and a claim with no source is marked "our reading".
No image on this site is AI-generated. The globes are NASA imagery and the terrain pictures are drawn from the elevation data.
